summary: Marisol Okafor, a retired ferry pilot, describes the last winter crossing of the Gannet Strait before the old route closed. She talks about navigating by foghorn echoes, the deckhand who taught her to read the tide table, and why she still keeps the ship's brass bell in her kitchen.

Two beekeepers in the Harrow Valley explain why their hives were moved onto a rooftop in the middle of town. They compare the honey from the rooftop with honey from the orchard, and describe what the bees do differently when the lime trees bloom.

A conversation with Teodor Lindqvist, who repairs mechanical clocks for a living, about a tower clock that ran four minutes slow for sixty years. He explains how the town grew used to the error and what happened on the day he fixed it.

The hosts visit a village library that lends out tools, seeds and sewing machines as well as books. The librarian, Priya Nandakumar, walks through how the lending rules were written and which item has never once come back.

A listener mailbag episode. Three listeners write in about night-shift habits: a baker who eats dinner at 4 a.m., a nurse who keeps a second set of curtains, and a ferry mechanic who listens to the show at the end of every shift.

Ines Calderon, a cartographer, talks about redrawing the coastline map of a small island after a storm moved a sandbar. She describes surveying on foot at low tide and how the islanders argued about what to name the new strip of sand.
